chapters.title: A New Practice for a New Reality
chapters.hook: Your brain is not tired from the work, it is tired from holding every loose promise at once.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people assume overload comes from having too much to do. Allen’s sharper claim is that vague, unparked commitments create the strain: the court call, school form, sink leak, and invoice all keep tugging until each has a visible place you trust.
chapters.tryThisNow: Take out your phone and open your notes app. Write down the first three things that are nagging at you right now, then save it. Notice how it feels to get them out of your head.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When email, errands, and meetings all tug at once, treat the stress as unnamed commitments, ask the next action, and park each reminder in a trusted place you will revisit.

breakdown.fastRead:
Halfway through a client call, printer ink, a school form, and the email you never answered walk into your head. None of them belongs in that call. Still, each one taps your shoulder.

That is an open loop: a promise your head is trying to hold because you have not put it anywhere reliable. The fix is not more effort. Your head is a bad shelf. Collect the loose items, put them where you will look again, then ask: what is this, and what can I do next? A loop stops shouting when it has a place to wait and a next action attached.
breakdown.deepRead:
After a packed arraignment morning, a public defender opens seven case files, and every folder presses back. Call a client. Check a plea offer. Find a missing address. Confirm a court date. The feeling is not evidence that she is failing. It is what happens when promises sit in the mind without shape. A missed date is not just a bad note in a file; it can mean more time in jail for a person waiting on her next move.

The pattern is simple and stubborn. Your attention keeps returning to anything it believes you may lose. If a commitment has no trusted place to live, your mind brings it back at bad times. If it has no clear next action, it stays too large to move. “Prepare case” is a cloud. “Email investigator for body-cam status” gives you a handle.

A trusted external system is simply a place you believe you will revisit: an inbox, a list, a calendar, a case note, a tray on the desk. It does not do your thinking for you. It lets memory stop pretending to be the whole system. Once the item is parked, you can decide what it means.

The same shift helps at home on Sunday night. Two parents are not really arguing about character when asthma medication, school forms, and a leaking sink collide. They are arguing among loose reminders. The useful questions are plain: What is this? What outcome do we need? Who has the next action? Where will the reminder live?

Relief comes before completion. You may still have a hard week, but now the work has edges. Edges tell you where to put your hand first.
breakdown.fullRead:
Imagine an air-traffic controller trying to hold every aircraft in memory: altitude, heading, speed, runway, clearance, weather, fuel. No competent person would call that focus. It would be negligence with a brave expression. The strip board, radar screen, and procedures do not replace judgment. They give judgment a clean field to work on.

Your workday has its own traffic. Some of it is formal, like a contract review or a board packet. Some of it arrives as a hallway request, a lab result, a child’s inhaler refill, a donor email, or a sticky note in a jacket pocket. The trouble is not simply the number of inputs. The trouble is that they arrive as stuff, half message and half obligation, and your mind tries to keep them all active.

A commitment becomes mentally expensive when three things are missing: a captured place, a desired result, and a next physical action. Without capture, you worry you will lose it. Without a result, you cannot tell when it is done. Without a next action, you cannot start without thinking through the whole matter again. So the same item appears at lunch, in the car, and at 2:17 a.m., each time asking to be decided from scratch.

High-level planning often fails when the runway is cluttered. A clean mission statement cannot tell you whether to call the school nurse, approve the invoice, or ask the client for the signed page. Purpose matters, but purpose has to meet a Monday morning. The practical move is humbler: collect every loose item, clarify what each one means, put the reminder where it belongs, and review the whole picture often enough that you trust it.

Consider a restaurant line cook newly responsible for festival prep. “Handle prep” sounds like work, but it is not yet an action. After service falls behind, the failure is easy to misread as poor effort. The better read is more specific: produce orders, station counts, sauce batches, and vendor calls were living as verbal fog. While they stayed there, servers apologized and guests waited. Once each promise has an owner, a due point, and a visible next step, the kitchen has something to execute.

The same discipline protects quieter work. A museum registrar checking loan paperwork cannot let every shipping question and donor email hijack the insurance checklist. One missed document can put a borrowed object and a professional relationship at risk. Each arrival needs a brief landing place before it earns attention. A rural veterinarian between farm visits faces the mobile version: lab results, medication questions, invoices, and client promises crossing county roads in the front seat. Fatigue grows when each one must be carried by memory from place to place.

Watch the edge. A system can become another place to hide. If you spend more time polishing lists than moving the next action, the list has begun to compete with the work. The test is not whether the system looks elegant. The test is whether it lets you stop remembering at the wrong time and choose clearly at the right one.

The first practice is not speed. It is containment. Get the loose promises out of your head, decide what each one is, name the next visible action, and place the reminder where you will see it when it can matter. Your mind is for choosing the runway, not for carrying every aircraft in the sky.

examples.title: Keiko Opens the Arraignment Files After Lunch

planSpec.domain: a public defender opening case files after a crowded arraignment morning
planSpec.audience: a public defender carrying too many client promises at once
planSpec.stakes: whether a court deadline or client follow-up gets missed because every case feels equally urgent
planSpec.requiredBeat: the defender stops treating the pressure as a character flaw and sees each worry as an open loop that needs a visible holding place before it can be judged

examples.scenario: Keiko slides into the public defender bullpen at 12:35 p.m., jacket still damp from the walk back from arraignments. Six new case files fan across her desk, each with a sticky note: call mother, request video, check immigration risk, confirm clinic letter. Before lunch she blamed the tightness in her chest on being bad at the job. After the second file, she sees the worries as unparked promises. She must decide whether to keep rereading or capture each one in a visible inbox first.
examples.whatToDo: Capture every client promise and court follow-up on one intake sheet before ranking them. Write the client name, desired result, next physical action, and where you will review it.
examples.whyItMatters: Until the promises are outside her head, the files compete as noise. A visible holding place lets deadlines, waiting items, and calls become separate choices instead of one alarm.

examples.title: Nereida Sorts the Sink, Forms, and Inhaler

planSpec.domain: two parents coordinating asthma medication, school forms, and a leaking sink on Sunday evening
planSpec.audience: a parent who feels household work is everywhere and nowhere
planSpec.stakes: whether a child's health routine and school paperwork are protected without turning the evening into blame
planSpec.requiredBeat: the conversation shifts from accusing someone of forgetting to asking what each loose item is, what needs to be true, and where the reminder will live

examples.scenario: Sunday, 8:17 p.m., Nereida and Samir stand in the kitchen. The spacer dries by the sink, a wet towel sits under the U-bend, and a school packet is crumpled by the toaster. "You forgot the inhaler form again," Samir says. "And you forgot the landlord," Nereida snaps. Then she stops. "What are the loose things? What needs to be true? Where does each reminder live?" Samir reaches for a marker.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the blame loop. Name each loose item aloud, define the wanted result, then write the reminder where both parents will see it: meds checklist, school folder, landlord call list.
examples.whyItMatters: Household commitments arrive as fragments from cabinets, backpacks, and pipes. Until each fragment has a visible container, both parents must remember everything, so every miss looks personal.

examples.title: Zuleikha Rebuilds Thursday Prep After the Festival Rush

planSpec.domain: a restaurant line cook newly responsible for prep before a festival weekend
planSpec.audience: a first-time kitchen lead whose work now includes invisible coordination
planSpec.stakes: whether missing produce orders and vague verbal requests cause service delays and food waste
planSpec.requiredBeat: the cook sees that 'handle prep' failed because it was not a defined commitment with a next visible action, owner, and trusted reminder

examples.scenario: At 11:18 p.m. Sunday, Zuleikha, a line cook turned weekend prep lead, sits on an overturned milk crate behind the fry station, reading the waste log from the festival rush: three cases of basil wilted, no backup pickles, two servers waiting on 86'd lamb sliders. On the prep clipboard, Thursday's note still says, "handle prep." She used it like a reminder to try harder. Now she sees it was never a commitment: no first action, no owner for produce, no place she checked before ordering.
examples.whatToDo: Rewrite "handle prep" as separate captured commitments: call the produce vendor by 10 a.m., assign each station's backup batch, check par sheets at close, and put every reminder on the prep board she reviews.
examples.whyItMatters: Prep crosses shifts, vendors, storage, and service timing. A vague label cannot trigger the right person at the right moment. A visible reminder can be reviewed before scarcity reaches the line.

examples.title: Caoimhe Tests the Strip Board at 4:17

planSpec.domain: an air-traffic control strip board compared with a controller trying to remember every aircraft unaided
planSpec.audience: a reader skeptical that writing things down changes anything
planSpec.stakes: whether the reader grasps that external systems reduce mental load without doing the thinking for you
planSpec.requiredBeat: the example makes the point that trusted containers do not replace judgment; they keep memory from becoming the runway

examples.scenario: Caoimhe stands in the tower cab at 4:17 p.m., a strip board in front of her showing six inbound flights and two departures. Now take the board away. She must hold call signs, altitudes, headings, fuel notes, and runway sequence in her head while a pilot asks for a change. She is about to decide which aircraft turns first. The strips have not made that call for her. They have kept memory off the runway long enough for judgment to work.
examples.whatToDo: Write each active aircraft, altitude, request, and constraint onto a visible strip before sequencing. Then look at the board and make the spacing decision from the whole picture.
examples.whyItMatters: Sequencing depends on comparing moving constraints at once. If the controller stores them in memory, recall competes with judgment and the weakest reminder can steer the choice.

examples.title: Marjan Catches the Donor Emails Before They Scatter

planSpec.domain: a museum registrar preparing loan paperwork while donor emails and shipping questions arrive
planSpec.audience: an arts administrator handling precise work amid constant interruptions
planSpec.stakes: whether insurance terms and shipping dates for a valuable artwork are handled cleanly instead of scattered across attention
planSpec.requiredBeat: the registrar captures new inputs as 'stuff' to clarify rather than letting each arrival hijack the current checklist

examples.scenario: Marjan is at the registrar's table in the conservation office at 4:15 p.m., comparing the loan agreement for a 1912 oil painting with the insurer's rider. A donor email pops up about a promised credit line, then the shipper texts, "Crate pickup Tuesday or Wednesday?" Her hand hovers over the email reply box. She must decide whether to chase each arrival now or drop both into her inbox as stuff to clarify after the insurance checklist is complete.
examples.whatToDo: Capture each new email or text in one inbox with a short note, then return to the loan checklist. Clarify the donor credit and pickup date when this review block ends.
examples.whyItMatters: Insurance terms need uninterrupted comparison. Donor notes and shipping questions are undefined commitments, so a visible holding place preserves them without making memory run the checklist.

examples.title: Belen Parks Promises Between Farm Calls

planSpec.domain: a rural veterinarian returning calls between farm visits with lab results, invoices, and medication questions in play
planSpec.audience: a mobile professional whose commitments arrive away from a desk
planSpec.stakes: whether animal care, client trust, and billing accuracy survive a day spent in motion
planSpec.requiredBeat: the vet notices that fatigue comes less from the number of calls than from carrying unparked promises across locations

examples.scenario: Belen Valcarce sits in her dented pickup at the edge of the Morrow dairy lot, boots still wet from the calf barn. Her phone shows nine callbacks: a potassium result for a ewe, two invoice questions, a mare's refill, and three owners who only said "call me." She rubs her eyes and realizes the calls are not the heavy part. The heavy part is carrying each promise in her head from gravel lane to gravel lane.
examples.whatToDo: Capture each call as soon as it lands: client, animal, issue, desired result, and next physical step. Put it in one return-call list Belen checks at every stop, not in memory.
examples.whyItMatters: Calls arrive in barns, trucks, and yards, but follow-up happens later. A visible list keeps care, billing, and medication promises from scattering across locations.

questions.prompt: An emergency dispatcher ends a shift with three items: a completed call log, a dentist appointment already on the calendar, and a vague worry to “check the staffing issue.” Which one most needs capture before going home?
choices: The vague staffing concern with no defined place to return to it.
The completed call log, since it involved serious work.
The dentist appointment, since personal items are easy to forget.
questions.explanation: The vague staffing concern is an unfinished commitment with no parked reminder. A completed log is closed, and a recorded appointment already has a trusted place to resurface.

questions.prompt: A university club treasurer keeps thinking about reimbursements during dinner, even after deciding to “deal with them tomorrow.” What best explains why the thought keeps returning?
choices: The forms are probably unimportant, so the mind keeps testing whether to ignore them.
The commitment is not in a place the treasurer reliably reviews.
Money tasks require more motivation than ordinary tasks.
questions.explanation: A mental promise to handle it later does not reassure the mind. A reviewable reminder does. The issue is not importance or motivation, but an undefined commitment without a trusted home.

questions.prompt: An architect is finishing permit drawings when three client texts arrive with design tweaks, budget concerns, and a possible meeting time. What is the cleanest response?
choices: Stop the permit work and answer all three texts before any detail gets lost.
Ignore the texts until tomorrow, since the drawings are the real priority.
Capture the three inputs in one inbox, then clarify them when the current pass is done.
questions.explanation: Capture protects the new inputs without letting them seize the current work. Answering instantly fragments attention, while ignoring them relies on memory and leaves open loops loose.

questions.prompt: A florist preparing for a holiday rush hears, “Do something nicer for the window,” “Call the wholesaler,” and “Check the van.” What first move would reduce the mental pile?
choices: Write each item into a visible inbox before deciding details.
Rank the items by which one feels most stressful.
Keep repeating the list aloud until the rush is over.
questions.explanation: The first relief comes from getting the loose items out of the head and into view. Stress ranking still leaves them vague, and rehearsal uses memory as the storage system.

questions.prompt: A sales rep leaves a client meeting with “send pricing,” “ask legal,” and “maybe samples next month” scribbled in the margin of a brochure. What should happen next?
choices: File the brochure with client materials so the notes stay connected to the account.
Clarify each note into an outcome or next physical action and park it on the right list.
Wait until the client follows up, since that will reveal what actually matters.
questions.explanation: Margins are not a reliable system. Clarifying creates usable reminders. Filing hides the work, and waiting lets the client become the reminder, which is risky and reactive.

questions.prompt: A city librarian has sticky notes on the desk, email flags, a notebook list, and a memory of a patron request. Nothing is huge, but everything feels loud. What is the main problem?
choices: The librarian has too many responsibilities for one role.
The tasks lack enough emotional urgency to drive action.
The commitments are scattered across places that are not reviewed as one system.
questions.explanation: The volume is less important than the scattered storage. A single reviewable system lowers noise. More urgency would add stress, and the role may be manageable once reminders are gathered.

questions.prompt: A film producer has a master list sorted by “important,” but is in a taxi with 12 minutes, no laptop, and low energy. The top item is a budget spreadsheet. What does this reveal?
choices: A good list must be filtered by context, time, and energy, not importance alone.
The producer should force the top item anyway to build trust in the list.
The list should only include quick tasks that can be done anywhere.
questions.explanation: Importance alone does not choose the next action. Current tools, time, and energy matter. Forcing the spreadsheet ignores reality, while listing only quick tasks loses larger commitments.

questions.prompt: A bakery owner missed an insurance renewal after keeping reminders in email, paper mail, and memory. Which fix is strongest?
choices: Put only renewal dates on the calendar and leave other business reminders where they are.
Create one capture path, clarify each item, and review the full inventory weekly.
Ask staff to remind the owner whenever they notice paperwork piling up.
questions.explanation: The strongest fix repairs the whole reminder chain: capture, clarify, organize, review. Calendar-only handles dates, not all commitments, and staff reminders are uneven substitutes for trust.

questions.prompt: A caregiver at the pharmacy remembers a lab question, a rideshare receipt, and a request to schedule physical therapy. The checkout line is moving. What should they do first?
choices: Call the clinic immediately so the medical item does not get buried.
Try to memorize the three items until reaching the car.
Put all three into a quick capture place that will be reviewed later.
questions.explanation: Quick capture prevents loss without forcing decisions in a checkout line. Calling one item leaves the others loose, and memorizing keeps the head responsible for storage.

reviewCards.front: You feel tense because five small promises are circling in your head at once. What first move should you make?
reviewCards.back: Diagnose overload as undefined commitments and externalize each one into a place you will revisit. Do not solve them yet. Get each promise out of your head and into a visible inbox so your mind can stop reheating it.

reviewCards.front: A nurse ends a shift with lab calls, family questions, and supply requests still in mind. How should she lower the mental load?
reviewCards.back: Treat each worry as an open loop, not as proof she is failing. Capture each item in a trusted place, then later clarify what it means, what outcome is needed, and what the next physical action is.

reviewCards.front: Your manager says, "Keep an eye on the vendor issue," and you feel the phrase stick in your head. What do you do with it?
reviewCards.back: Turn the vague request into a defined commitment. Ask what needs to be true, who owns it, and what the next visible action is. Then park the reminder in a place you will actually check, instead of carrying the phrase around.

reviewCards.front: You are voting on a local school measure, but your mind keeps jumping to taxes, emails, and dinner plans. What is the clean move?
reviewCards.back: First clear the stray commitments from your head into an inbox you trust. Then return to the choice in front of you. Externalizing the loose loops does not decide the vote, it frees attention so you can judge the issue instead of the noise.

reviewCards.front: A coach remembers equipment forms, parent texts, and a player injury while watching practice. Why does writing them down help?
reviewCards.back: Writing them down gives memory a container, not a substitute for judgment. Once each commitment is external and reviewable, the coach can keep watching the field, then later decide what each item means and what action belongs next.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is turning mental noise into captured commitments. When a worry, promise, request, or idea appears, you do not try to remember it or solve it at once. You put it in a visible place you check, so your mind can stop reheating it and you can decide later what it means.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a request arrives while you are already working on something, then write the request in one inbox with the sender, date, and any promised follow-up before returning to the current task.
If you notice a household worry repeating in your head, then write it as a plain item in your capture place, such as call plumber about sink leak or buy inhaler refill.
If someone says we need to talk about this later, then ask for ten seconds to capture the topic and where you will revisit it, instead of relying on one of you to remember.
If a medication question, appointment detail, or lab result concern comes up away from your desk, then put it in your phone or notebook immediately with the next place you will check it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For ten minutes today, empty your head onto one sheet or note. Capture every loose promise, worry, errand, message, form, bill, and idea without sorting it yet.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, spend twenty minutes clearing your capture places. Look at each item and decide what it is, whether anything must happen, and where the reminder belongs next.

memorableLines.text: Your brain is not tired from the work, it is tired from holding every loose promise at once.
memorableLines.why: It reframes exhaustion as the burden of unparked promises rather than volume—a diagnosis readers immediately recognize.

memorableLines.text: Relief comes before completion.
memorableLines.why: This unexpected reversal challenges the assumption that relief comes only after finishing, making it quotable and surprising.

memorableLines.text: Your mind is for choosing the runway, not for carrying every aircraft in the sky.
memorableLines.why: The metaphor shows the mind's actual purpose rather than its current burden, making it both clarifying and memorable.

chapters.title: Getting Control of Your Life: The Five Stages of Mastering Workflow
chapters.hook: The scrap in your pocket is not small until it has passed through a place you trust.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people try to feel in control by ranking what is already shouting. Allen starts earlier: capture first, then decide what each item means, where it belongs, and when you will see it again. Priority works only after the workflow stops leaking.
chapters.tryThisNow: In the next minute, pick one task from your to-do list. Write down the next physical action you can take to move it forward. Place it in a visible spot to remind you.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When email, errands, and meeting notes blur together, run each item through capture, clarify, organize, review, and engage so your next choice comes from trusted reminders, not memory.

breakdown.fastRead:
Your phone buzzes in the middle of dinner. You remember printer ink, a school form, and a client reply. None of it is hard. Still, your head gets loud. Those are open loops: small promises your brain keeps handing back because you have not put them anywhere reliable.

Relief starts when each thing has a place to wait. Do not sort it in your head over salad. First catch every loose thing in one inbox. Then ask: What is it? What would done look like? What physical move would start it? Put the reminder on a list, on a date, or in the trash. A thing is under control only when you know what it is, what done means, and where it can wait without shouting.
breakdown.deepRead:
You can see the problem in a band director standing in the hallway with coffee in one hand and three new requests in the other: a parent email about rides, a trumpet repair slip, and a note from the principal about concert chairs. If all three land on one giant list called "spring concert," the list may look complete and still leave a student waiting after rehearsal.

Control starts before planning. Capture means every loose item goes into a container you will empty: an inbox tray, a notebook, or a voice memo. You are not deciding yet. You are getting the work out of memory and into a place that will hold it. Capture works only if you collect everything, keep the number of collection places low, and empty them often enough to trust them.

Then clarify. Take one item at a time. Is it actionable? Can someone do something about it now? If not, it is trash, reference, or maybe later. If yes, choose the path: do it if it takes two minutes, delegate it if someone else owns it, or defer it onto a list or calendar.

Organize gives the reminder a home. The parent email becomes "Call bus office about extra van." The trumpet slip becomes waiting for: "repair quote from music shop." The chair note becomes a calendar item for Thursday. A clean list is not a bigger pile. It is a set of reminders parked where you will actually see them.

Now picture a repair technician stuck at Gate C17 with thirty minutes and a low battery. Because the work has already been clarified, the choice is sane. Phone calls fit the airport. A parts form can wait for the laptop. A hard estimate can wait for higher energy. Engage means choosing from work you have already made clear, instead of asking a tired brain to reload the whole day.
breakdown.fullRead:
After a bad Saturday dinner rush, a new shift lead can feel blame tighten the whole restaurant. The walk-in was short on basil. Two servers asked about next week’s schedule. The prep list had "sauce" on it, which helped no one at 7:15. Everyone worked hard. The work still had no reliable route.

Here is the quiet point of workflow control: effort is not the same as closure. Work becomes manageable when every incoming thing passes through five stages in order: capture, clarify, organize, review, and engage. Skip one, and the pressure shows up somewhere else.

Capture is the first kindness. It says, "Not now, but not lost." A hospital charge nurse emptying scrub pockets at the end of a shift is not being fussy when she drops a family callback, a medication question, and a supply request into one visible place before judging them. If she judges while collecting, the item with the loudest emotion wins. If she collects first, every commitment gets seen. For the family waiting on the callback, the reminder is not office clutter. It is the next time they know what is happening.

Clarify is where vague concern gets converted into meaning. "Handle Rivera matter" is not work yet for a public defender leaving a crowded arraignment calendar. It is a worry with a case name attached. Clarifying asks two blunt questions: What outcome would make this done, and what visible action would move it forward? "File amended motion by Friday" is an outcome. "Email clerk for the missing transcript" is an action. Rereading the note is not.

Organize protects the decision you just made. Actionable items do not belong in one mixed pile. If it takes two minutes, do it and remove it from the system. If someone else owns it, delegate it and track the waiting-for. If it must happen on a certain day or time, put it on the calendar. If it can be done as soon as you are in the right setting, put it on the right action list. Non-actionable items need homes too: trash, reference, or maybe later. A clean system makes "not now" different from "forgotten."

Review is where trust is repaired. Lists go stale faster than people admit. A Friday scan by a warehouse supervisor before an inventory audit can surface the missing vendor confirmation, the unfilled Tuesday shift, and the pallet count nobody updated. Without review, lists become old promises in tidy rows. With review, they become a current map. The Weekly Review is the larger reset, the time to look across projects, waiting-fors, calendars, and next actions until the whole inventory feels real again.

Engage is last for a reason. You cannot choose well from an unclear pile. Once the work has been captured, clarified, organized, and reviewed, the question changes from "What am I afraid of forgetting?" to "What can I do from here?" A traveling technician in an airport delay may have a phone, thirty minutes, and low energy. That is enough for two callbacks, not enough for a careful repair report. Context, time, energy, and priority narrow the choice without drama.

There are edges. Too many inboxes recreate the same mess with better labels. A two-minute rule can become a trap if you use it to dodge larger commitments all day. A list you never review will not earn your mind’s trust, no matter how neat it looks. The test is simple: when a homeowner asks a building inspector what happens after a storm visit, can the answer name the item, the desired result, the reminder’s home, and the next contact?

The five stages are not a personality upgrade. They are a sequence for moving work out of your head and into places that can hold it. Capture before you judge. Clarify before you sort. Organize before you review. Review before you choose. Engage with the item in front of you only when the rest of the pile has a trusted place to wait.

examples.title: Marika Empties Her Pockets Before Handoff

planSpec.domain: a hospital charge nurse clearing end-of-shift scraps from pockets and handoff notes
planSpec.audience: a nurse responsible for keeping patient follow-ups from disappearing between shifts
planSpec.stakes: whether a family callback, medication question, or supply request gets lost because it stayed as a half-memory
planSpec.requiredBeat: the nurse captures every loose reminder into one visible inbox before deciding importance, showing that collection comes before judgment

examples.scenario: Marika is the charge nurse on 4 West at 7:18 p.m., standing by the handoff printer with report starting in twelve minutes. Her scrub pockets hold a sticky note about Mr. Han’s daughter, a wrapper marked “ask pharmacy re: Lovenox,” and a supply card for pediatric IV tubing. She wants to triage them as she finds them, but stops, opens the red inbox tray, and drops every scrap and handoff note there first. Only then will she decide what matters tonight.
examples.whatToDo: Empty every pocket, clipboard, and handoff note into one tray before sorting. Then clarify each item as callback, med question, supply request, waiting, or next action.
examples.whyItMatters: Judging while collecting lets small reminders hide in separate places. One visible inbox creates a complete batch, so the handoff can be clarified from the same map.

examples.title: Kavitha Names the Rivera Filing on the Courthouse Steps

planSpec.domain: a public defender leaving a crowded arraignment calendar with vague case notes
planSpec.audience: a lawyer carrying many live obligations with court deadlines attached
planSpec.stakes: whether a client’s next filing stalls because 'handle Rivera matter' is not yet a defined outcome or action
planSpec.requiredBeat: the lawyer turns a vague note into the desired outcome and one next physical action instead of rereading it as if concern were progress

examples.scenario: Kavitha leaves Courtroom 3B at 11:55 with arraignment folders under one arm and her phone buzzing from the next calendar call. In the margin of one file she has written, “handle Rivera matter.” She rereads it twice, feeling responsible but no clearer. If she stops, she risks being late upstairs. If she runs, the note stays foggy. On the courthouse steps she writes: “Outcome: Rivera bail-modification filed by Friday. Next action: call clerk for transcript deadline before 2 p.m.”
examples.whatToDo: Stop rereading the vague note. Write the wanted result in plain words, then name the next physical move, such as calling the clerk, drafting the motion caption, or emailing the investigator.
examples.whyItMatters: Court work moves through deadlines, documents, and named handoffs. A vague concern cannot be calendared or reviewed, but a clear outcome and next action can enter the system before it disappears.

examples.title: Candelaria Sorts the Spring Concert Pile

planSpec.domain: a high school band director preparing for a spring concert while fielding permission slips, instrument repairs, and parent emails
planSpec.audience: a teacher who has many small commitments arriving through many channels
planSpec.stakes: whether concert logistics become a noisy pile or a set of reminders that can be found when needed
planSpec.requiredBeat: the director sorts clarified items into calendar, next-action, waiting-for, and reference places rather than keeping one mixed master list

examples.scenario: At 4:12 p.m. in the band room, Candelaria dumps a blazer pocket onto the timpani stool: six permission slips, a repair tag for a cracked bassoon joint, two parent emails open on her phone, and a program draft marked "ask custodians?" Last week she kept one frantic spring-concert list and still missed the trumpet mute order. This time, after naming each item, she puts the concert date on the calendar, the custodian email on next-actions, the bassoon tag on waiting-for, and the seating chart in reference.
examples.whatToDo: Clarify each scrap before filing it: calendar fixed dates, put visible tasks on next-action lists, park replies or repairs under waiting-for, and save stable details as reference.
examples.whyItMatters: A single master list mixes dates, actions, dependencies, and facts, so the next search happens under pressure. Separate containers let each reminder appear when its use condition is real.

examples.title: Qamar’s Friday Audit Map Before Lockup

planSpec.audience: an operations lead whose work depends on seeing the whole map before Monday starts
planSpec.stakes: whether missing vendor confirmations and staffing gaps surface early enough to fix
planSpec.requiredBeat: the supervisor reviews projects, waiting-fors, calendars, and action lists until the system feels current enough to stop mentally reheating the audit

examples.scenario: Qamar is the regional warehouse supervisor left in the office at 5:18 p.m. Friday, forklift beepers fading beyond the glass. He is about to shut his laptop, but next week's inventory audit keeps replaying: pallet counts, temp labor, vendor signoffs. He opens the project list, waiting-fors, Monday calendar, and action lists, updating each until the missing carton vendor reply and two unfilled scanner shifts are visible instead of buzzing in his head.
examples.whatToDo: Review the whole audit map before leaving: projects, waiting-fors, calendar, and action lists. Add missing vendor confirmations and staffing gaps where you will see them Monday.
examples.whyItMatters: Inventory audits fail at the seams between people, dates, and confirmations. A full Friday review makes those seams visible early enough to call, schedule, or reassign.

examples.title: Meilin Sorts Work at Gate C18
