The pile stays the same size; the noise drops.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is the reflex to write down any thought that carries a commitment the moment it appears, before deciding whether it matters or what to do about it. Over time this replaces the habit of mentally rehearsing unfinished items with a physical motion: something surfaces, you write it down, and you move on. The result is not a longer list but a quieter head. Your attention becomes available for the work in front of you instead of the work you are afraid to forget.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a colleague mentions something you will need to follow up on during a meeting or hallway conversation, then write it in your capture tool before the next person speaks, even if you are certain you will remember it.

If a partner, friend, or family member asks you for something and you say yes, then write it down before you reply to the next message or leave the room, so the commitment does not live only in the moment you made it.

If a doctor, dentist, or pharmacist gives you a verbal instruction you were not expecting, then write the exact instruction in your phone or notebook before you leave the building, not when you get home.

If a nagging thought surfaces while you are in the middle of something else (driving, cooking, lying in bed), then treat it as an item that belongs in a capture tool and write it down at the first safe moment rather than letting it replay until morning.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, set a timer for 15 minutes and write down every commitment currently living only in your head, one item per line, without stopping to sort or decide what any of it means. When the timer goes off, count the items.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, before you close your laptop or leave your workspace for the day, spend two minutes writing down anything you are holding in your head that does not yet live on a list or calendar. Add each item without processing it. Processing comes later. The goal is to finish the week with a clear mental holding area, not a perfect plan.

memorableLines.text: Every item you are mentally rehearsing right now is costing you something, and none of it is moving.
memorableLines.why: Names the invisible cost and futility of mental rehearsal in concrete terms that readers recognize immediately.

memorableLines.text: They are not confessing to a bad memory. They are transferring responsibility from a fallible organ to a reliable container.
memorableLines.why: Reframes capture as empowering transfer rather than weakness; the organ/container metaphor is specific and memorable.

memorableLines.text: Your mind was never supposed to hold the list. It was supposed to choose from it.
memorableLines.why: Compressed inversion that shifts how readers understand memory and work; would work as a social-media pull quote.

chapters.title: The Power of the Next-Action Decision
chapters.hook: Your list is full of things you care about and empty of things you can do.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people assume a stalled project means low motivation or too little time. It usually means the list item is an outcome disguised as a task, and no amount of caring moves an outcome. The moment you name the physical action, urgency becomes irrelevant: you either do it or you choose not to, and both are decisions you can actually make.
chapters.tryThisNow: Open the last task you postponed. What exact physical move would begin it? Say that answer out loud. Notice how much clearer the choice just got.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Replace every vague project state on your list with a specific physical action, the one thing you would do with your hands or a phone, so each item becomes chooseable instead of paralyzing.

breakdown.fastRead:
There's a task that's been on your list for three weeks. You look at it. You move past it. Nothing happens.

The problem is not that you do not care. The problem is that what you wrote is not a task. 'Follow up with Dana' is a hope. 'Email Dana asking whether she has questions about Section 3' is something you can do right now, with a keyboard, in ninety seconds.

Your brain does not get stuck on hard work. It gets stuck on blur. A vague item asks you to figure out what it means before you can do anything with it, and that figuring happens at the wrong moment, when your attention was already pointed somewhere else. Give it a physical step instead. A phone call to a real number. A specific email. A short question for someone in the next room.

One rule: if you cannot picture someone doing it with their body, it is not a next action yet.
breakdown.deepRead:
Picture two versions of Monday morning. In the first, you sit down with forty client items and stare. Every item is a project state: 'pending contract,' 'waiting on review,' 'translation in progress.' Three minutes pass. You open your phone.

In the second version, same list, same person, same morning, every item carries a next action. 'Email Karin asking for the revised source file.' 'Check the portal for client feedback on draft four.' Three minutes later, two emails are sent and you have started the third.

The difference is not motivation or energy. It is clarity. A vague item asks nothing specific of you. Before you can act, you have to work out what acting even means, and that decision costs the attention you were planning to spend on the work itself.

The fix asks you to slow down during capture, not during execution. For each item, two questions: what does done look like, and what is the next physical action? Not the next goal. Not a general direction. Something you do with a keyboard, a phone, a body in a specific room at a specific time.

You will discover which items are real commitments and which are wishes that found their way onto a list. The principal whose list reads 'handle fire drill compliance' has not planned anything. She has postponed the planning decision, and if the district inspector shows up in three weeks, she will not be ready. The moment she writes 'call district safety office at ext. 4421 and ask which form they need by May 30,' the project becomes something that can be started.

That level of specificity is not perfectionism. It is the minimum required to make a task chooseable. From an action-level list, you can look at where you are, how much time remains, and pick what fits. From a vague list, you can only feel behind.
breakdown.fullRead:
Six months of work. A competitor released first. The postmortem starts with the usual question: what slipped?

The product team traces the timeline. Every milestone reads like an announcement: 'beta testing complete,' 'QA sign-off received,' 'press assets finalized.' It looks like a plan. But nobody ever wrote down whose job it was to call the QA vendor and book the testing slot. That call, two minutes on the phone, never appeared anywhere as an action to take. So nobody took it. The milestone waited, and the launch window closed.

What failed was not commitment. Everyone cared about the launch. What failed was the decision about what the commitment actually required of someone on a specific afternoon.

Next-action discipline does its real work here: not as personal productivity hygiene, but as a form of organizational clarity. A project moves when someone owns a physical action, not when everyone owns an outcome. 'Beta testing complete' belongs to the air. 'Call Henrik at QA and book a two-week slot starting the third week of April' belongs to a person with a phone.

The distinction sounds procedural, but it changes what sitting down with work feels like. A list of outcomes produces a low-level unease that is hard to name. You look at the items, you know you care, and you still do not start. That unease comes from the gap between where you are and where the items assume you already are. An outcome is set in an imagined future where someone has already figured out the steps. It cannot be done from here. Only a physical action can be done from here.

'Research countertops' sat on the nurse's list for four months. She was not procrastinating on the kitchen renovation. She was procrastinating on the decision of what researching countertops actually meant, because the item as written could mean anything from an afternoon lost to design sites to one supplier's page. When she finally wrote 'spend twenty minutes on one supplier's site, write down three product names, text them to the contractor,' the task lost its weight. It became small enough to do between shifts.

The edge case worth examining is the person who converts this into a ritual of list-making. They get good at writing action-level items. Their lists are precise and comprehensive. But nothing gets done, because the lists have become the hobby. The measure of the method is not list quality. It is whether you start more things and finish more things than you did before. A beautifully formatted list that you stare at rather than work from has failed the same test as a vague list, just more elegantly.

The discipline works because specificity removes the last decision standing between you and the work. Before you turned 'confirm the site visit with Brennan' into 'call Brennan Thursday morning and ask whether he wants to meet at the property or the office,' you had to make that choice at the moment of action, when your attention was already on something else. After, the choice is banked. You see what the action is, and you do it or you consciously decide not to, because you have other priorities. Both outcomes are better than the third option: looking at the item until you open your phone.

What you end up with, if you do this consistently, is not a productivity system. It is a map you can actually navigate. The items on it correspond to moves in the world, not states you hope to achieve someday. You can look at where you are, what tools you have, how much time remains in the afternoon, and pick something that fits. That kind of choosing is different from the panicked triage most people practice. It is calm. It comes from having done the thinking in advance, on purpose, so that the moment of action can be clean.

examples.title: Winifred Identifies the Real Action Behind a Stalled Proposal

planSpec.domain: a staffing consultant reviewing client proposals at her home desk at 6:45 PM on a Friday
planSpec.audience: a self-employed consultant who bills by project and manages her own pipeline

examples.scenario: Winifred is at her home desk at 6:45 on a Friday, two browser tabs of proposal drafts open, a half-eaten dinner still on the counter. examples.whatToDo: Replace 'handle fire drill documentation' with 'call district safety office at ext. 4421 and ask which form they need submitted by May 30.' One phone number makes it startable.
examples.whyItMatters: A vague item cannot be scheduled, delegated, or started. Naming the specific call removes every decision except when to pick up the phone.

examples.whyItMatters: A vague item has no entry point. It reappears on every list because there is nothing to start. A named action with a duration and a destination gives the work a body your schedule can actually hold.

questions.prompt: A school librarian has 'library renovation' on her project list and wants to take the next step today. Of the following, which entry is a next physical action?
choices: Email the facilities coordinator asking whether the shelving quote from February is still valid.
Plan the renovation timeline and coordinate with all stakeholders.
Research the renovation needs and create a comprehensive scope of work.
questions.explanation: A next physical action is something you can do with your body right now: composing and sending a specific email. The other two describe outcomes or phases that themselves require further definition before anything can move.

questions.prompt: A freelance graphic designer has had 'sort out the Kimura account' on her list for three weeks. She is not procrastinating and the client relationship is still active. What most likely explains why the item keeps carrying forward without progress?
choices: The project has too much emotional weight for her to engage with it objectively.
The item describes an outcome rather than a physical action, so there is no specific step to start.
The list is too long and this item keeps getting buried beneath more urgent work.
questions.explanation: Vague outcome language like 'sort out' gives the brain no physical starting point. Without a concrete first action, the mind skips over it each review. Emotional weight and list length are plausible but secondary: the core problem is that the item has not been translated into something doable.

questions.prompt: A physical therapy clinic owner has 'deal with the billing software problem' on her list. She sits down to work on it Monday morning and feels immediately stuck. What is the most useful move she can make right now?
choices: Move it to a someday list since it is clearly not ready to act on yet.
Block two hours on her calendar for a billing software deep-dive later this week.
Call the billing software's support line and describe the specific error message she last saw.
questions.explanation: The item stalls because it has no defined physical action. Calling support with a specific description is a concrete step she can take right now. Moving it to someday postpones the problem; blocking calendar time trades one vague commitment for another without adding clarity.

questions.prompt: A parks coordinator comparing two list versions before her workday: Version A lists 'playground safety audit' and 'expand dog park outreach.' Version B lists 'call the adjuster at ext. 340 to confirm which inspection form is current' and 'post the survey link to the neighborhood group.' Which version lets her begin work immediately?
choices: Version B, because each item is a physical action she can start without further translation.
Version A, because high-level items keep her focused on the bigger picture and prevent premature tunnel vision.
Neither, because both versions are missing due dates, which are what actually trigger action.
questions.explanation: Version B contains physical actions: a specific call, a specific post. Each can begin immediately. Version A contains outcomes that each require a second round of thinking before anything moves. Due dates help with scheduling but do not replace a defined next action.

questions.prompt: At a nonprofit board meeting, the executive director says 'fundraising strategy for Q3' has been on the agenda for six weeks without movement. One board member suggests the group needs stronger commitment to the goal. A second suggests scheduling a longer planning retreat. What would most likely actually unblock it?
choices: Agreeing on a hard deadline for the full fundraising plan and holding each member accountable for their section.
Naming a single specific action one specific person will complete before the next meeting, and writing it down.
Breaking the strategy into sub-goals and assigning each sub-goal to a committee for ownership.
questions.explanation: Six weeks of stalling usually means the item is an outcome with no defined physical next action and no single owner. Naming one action and one owner gives the loop a real closing move. Deadlines on vague commitments create pressure without motion; sub-goals are still outcomes that need their own next actions before anything moves.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic manager has three items on her desk: (1) 'improve the client reminder system,' (2) 'think through whether to hire a part-time receptionist,' and (3) 'call VetSoft and ask whether their SMS module can send 48-hour notices.' Which items are next physical actions?
choices: Items 1 and 2, because both describe real work she intends to do.
All three, because they all represent commitments she plans to act on.
Item 3 only, because it names a specific physical interaction she can perform right now.
questions.explanation: A next physical action must be concrete enough to start without further definition. Item 3 names a specific call with a specific question. Item 1 is a project outcome. Item 2 uses 'think through,' which sounds active but needs further definition before any physical step can begin.

questions.prompt: A product team ran a retrospective and found their milestone tracker listed every deliverable as an outcome: 'user testing complete,' 'backend integration done,' 'design review finished.' The product shipped three weeks late. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
choices: The tracker recorded project state rather than defining who would do what next, leaving responsibility for starting each phase implicit and unowned.
The team lacked engineering capacity and needed to hire earlier in the planning cycle.
The project was over-scoped and the team should have cut features rather than changed their tracking format.
questions.explanation: Outcome-only trackers show progress history but do not define next moves. When a milestone says 'testing complete,' nobody is prompted to own the action that starts testing. The lateness stems from implicit handoffs, not headcount or scope, though those may be contributing factors.

questions.prompt: A homeowner has written 'replace the bathroom exhaust fan' on his task list nine times over four months. He owns the house, has free weekends, and does not find the task emotionally difficult. Why does the item most likely keep reappearing?
choices: The task is low priority and his system is correctly deferring it in favor of more urgent items.
He has not found the right tool for tracking home maintenance and keeps losing the carry-forward.
He has not defined a next physical action, so each review finds it still open and copies it forward without progress.
questions.explanation: Repeated carry-forwards without progress signal an item never translated into a physical action. Without a specific step (measure the fan, look up a model, order from a supplier), each review copies the same vague entry forward. Priority and tool choice do not explain persistence when someone has time and no emotional block.

questions.prompt: A lab manager picking between two tracking approaches with a grant deadline six weeks away: Approach A records outcome statements and weekly sub-goals that team members update. Approach B records one current next physical action per person, updated each time one is completed. Which approach is more likely to keep the team moving?
choices: Approach A, because outcome statements are more durable than action lists, which go stale the moment someone completes a step.
Approach B, because each person always has a defined physical action available and can start without another planning conversation.
Approach A, because sub-goals give team members a richer sense of the project arc and help them make better local decisions.
questions.explanation: With a real deadline, the team needs action, not more planning. Approach B gives each person a concrete next step at all times. Approach A's sub-goals are still outcomes: someone must still define what to do first. Updating actions when completed is the model, not a flaw.

reviewCards.front: You have 'fix the client relationship' sitting on your list for three weeks. It has not moved. What is the first thing to do with it?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the next physical action is: something you can do with your body, a phone, a keyboard, or a person in front of you. 'Fix the client relationship' is an outcome, not an action. Rewrite it as one specific step, like 'text Rafael asking for a 15-minute call this week.'

reviewCards.front: Your weekly list has 'deal with the contractor situation.' You keep skipping it. What is the most likely reason, and what do you do about it?
reviewCards.back: You skip vague items because your brain cannot start something undefined. Translate it: decide what done looks like, then write the one physical step that starts the clock, like 'call the contractor at the number on the invoice and ask for a revised timeline.' The item was a category; you need an action.

reviewCards.front: Your teammate says she will 'handle the vendor renewal.' Three days pass, nothing moves. What question should have been asked before the meeting ended?
reviewCards.back: Ask what the next physical action is and who owns it. 'Handle the vendor renewal' is a project, not a task. Before the meeting ends, pin down a sentence like: 'Lars will email the vendor rep today asking for a renewal quote.' Vague ownership of a vague item produces reliable inaction.

reviewCards.front: Your app launch slipped three weeks. In the postmortem, every item on the milestone tracker turns out to be an outcome. What would a better list have looked like?
reviewCards.back: Outcome items tell you what done looks like but give no one a place to start. A list built from next physical actions assigns the first step to a specific person when the item is created. The phone call to the QA vendor, the email to the press contact: each has an owner and a verb. The gap between a milestone tracker and a next-action list is often exactly the length of a delay.

reviewCards.front: You finally sit down to work and your list has forty items. You stare at it for three minutes, then check your phone instead. What is wrong with the list?
reviewCards.back: A list you cannot start from is a list of outcomes and categories, not actions. Each item should be a physical move you can begin without deciding further. Scan for items with no clear verb or with vague verbs like 'address' or 'follow up.' Rewrite each one as something you can do right now: open a browser, dial a number, write a first sentence.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is converting any vague item on a list into one specific physical move: a call, a click, a message, a walk to a specific room. Most list items stall not because you are avoiding them but because they are outcomes written as if they were actions, and a vague item cannot be started. When you can translate commitment into motion consistently, choosing what to do next stops feeling like a judgment call and starts feeling like reading a menu.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a meeting ends with phrases like 'we need to figure out X' or 'someone should look into Y,' then ask out loud before the call ends: who has the next action and what exactly will they do? One two-minute question prevents three weeks of circular email.

If a home or errand item has appeared on your list more than twice without moving, then rewrite its entry as a sentence starting with a physical verb plus a specific location, name, or number, as if you are leaving instructions for someone who does not know your house or your contacts.

If you catch yourself thinking 'I really need to get back to this person,' then open a message to them in that moment and type one sentence before you decide whether to send it. Drafting breaks the loop that keeps the thought circling back.

If a financial item like 'sort out insurance' or 'deal with the tax thing' has sat on your list for more than a week, then identify the single call or form that starts the process and replace the vague phrase with that call or form as the actual item.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, open your list or notes app and find one item written as a noun or a vague phrase like 'kitchen project' or 'proposal thing.' Rewrite it as a single sentence starting with a physical verb and ending with enough detail that a stranger could do it without asking you a question.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, spend ten minutes scanning your active list for items that describe an outcome rather than an action. For each one, write the single physical move that would start it. This is not a planning session but a translation pass. Your goal is to end with a list where every item can be started within sixty seconds of reading it.

memorableLines.text: Your list is full of things you care about and empty of things you can do.
memorableLines.why: Opens with surgical precision on the real problem—motivation is not the issue, the lack of doable items is.

memorableLines.text: Your brain does not get stuck on hard work. It gets stuck on blur.
memorableLines.why: Surprising inversion that names something true but counterintuitive; the source of procrastination is not difficulty but ambiguity.

memorableLines.text: An outcome is set in an imagined future where someone has already figured out the steps. It cannot be done from here. Only a physical action can be done from here.
memorableLines.why: The chapter's fulcrum sentence; explains why naming a physical action actually works—it removes the last decision between you and the work.

chapters.title: The Power of Outcome Focusing
chapters.hook: You cannot track a commitment that has no close condition, and most of yours do not have one.
chapters.counterintuition: Most people assume the problem is not knowing what to do next. It is not. The problem is that 'done' was never defined, so the system has nothing to track toward and the mind keeps the loop open regardless of how much action happens.
chapters.tryThisNow: Find the task you've been stuck on. Say what done is. One sentence. Then pick your first move. Notice what changed.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before picking any next action, write one sentence naming exactly what done looks like, so your system holds a concrete close condition instead of a vague open loop.

breakdown.fastRead:
You have had 'finish proposal' on your list for four days. It is still there. Not because you are avoiding it, but because you never said what finished looks like.

Your mind keeps that loop running until it sees a close condition. The list does not need more items. It needs one sentence that says where this one ends.

Write it before you touch the task. Something like: 'Draft sent to client with pricing and timeline, waiting for approval.' Now you can see the destination. The gap has edges now. The next step follows without argument.

That sentence is not planning. Without it, your list will run that loop forever.
breakdown.deepRead:
The planning meeting runs two hours. Everyone contributes. Nobody disagrees. Then someone asks for next steps, and the room goes quiet. Not from lack of motivation. Nobody had named what the meeting needed to produce. Without a declared end state, the group has no way to notice when it drifts and no finish line to cross.

Vague commitments do not just feel incomplete. They stay in rotation. Your mind holds them open because nothing in the list says where they end. Write a crisp end state and the vagueness has nowhere to hide. What to do next becomes visible, because done is now a place, not a feeling.

Consider a charge nurse at the end of a long shift. Her whiteboard says 'handle Room 14 discharge.' She has read it a dozen times. Nothing moves. Then she rewrites it: 'patient has signed paperwork, transport confirmed, bed flagged available.' Three steps surface in the next ten seconds. The outcome statement did not add facts she lacked. It organized what she already knew into something she could act on.

Vague items sit on lists because we tolerate motion without progress. Write the end state, and the tolerance disappears. You either have the thing or you do not. That is the only question your list ever needed to ask.
breakdown.fullRead:
Soren has 'revise dissertation' on his list for the second Sunday in a row. He opens the document, reads a paragraph, closes it, marks an hour as done. Nothing is moving. The item gives him nothing to aim at. He has no close condition written down, so his mind keeps the loop running.

The moment he writes one sentence, 'methods section revised, all committee notes addressed, version sent to advisor by Thursday,' two things happen at once: the low-grade background noise quiets, and the first concrete action surfaces. Not because the work got easier. Because he can see what is missing and what comes next.

People resist writing that sentence for a reason. A task labeled 'work on the dissertation' can be worked on forever without technically failing. 'Methods section revised' closes the gap in a way that 'revise dissertation' never does. The vagueness was not an accident. It was protection.

A declared outcome makes the distance measurable. Without a visible close condition, there is nothing to plan toward. With one, every decision has a referent: does this close the gap or not?

Declaring an outcome forces a moment of real thinking most people skip. You have to picture it clearly enough that someone else could verify it. Not a mood, not a category. A picture. Petra, a freelance translator, writes 'Müller contract' as a project entry and feels like she has handled it. The label holds anxiety at arm's length. When she replaces it with 'Müller legal brief returned with tracked changes accepted and final invoice sent,' the comfort disappears. She can see exactly how far the project is from done. The next step is visible: the brief goes out before the invoice.

The same problem scales without changing shape. A regional operations manager runs a full-day offsite to build a Q3 territory plan. Fourteen locations, a full agenda, lunch brought in. At the end: no plan. The postmortem traces back to one thing. The day had no declared end state, no sentence written before the room filled. Without that sentence, the group could not notice when it drifted, could not course-correct, could not close. They had a busy day. They did not have a productive offsite.

One distinction worth naming: a declared outcome is not the same as a plan. The outcome is the picture of done. The plan comes after, if you need one at all. Jumping from 'we should do something about this' straight into project planning often produces a plan aimed at a vague something. It feels thorough. It points in no particular direction.

The rule holds at any scale. A line cook developing a new menu section needs to picture five dishes listed, portion notes included, approved by the chef. A project coordinator needs to picture a signed scope document and a kickoff date on the calendar, not just 'onboard the client.' The deadline and the stakes differ. The structure does not.

Before touching any commitment, write one sentence describing what done looks like in terms someone else could verify. That sentence closes what your mind was keeping open. It makes the first physical action visible, because the gap now has edges.

Your list does not know whether you care. It knows whether the project has a declared end state. That is the only thing it needs to move.

examples.title: Senait Rewrites Room 14 Before the Night Nurse Arrives

planSpec.requiredBeat: she catches herself writing 'handle Room 14 discharge' and rewrites it as 'patient has signed paperwork, transport is confirmed, and bed is flagged available' — the outcome declared, the next phone call obvious

examples.scenario: Senait is thirty minutes from handover, standing at the six-room whiteboard with a red marker, and three patients are still pending discharge. Room 14 is medically cleared, and the paperwork is somewhere in the pile. She uncaps the marker and writes 'handle Room 14 discharge.' Her hand stops. examples.title: Leif Traces the Offsite Failure to One Missing Sentence

examples.scenario: Leif manages fourteen branch locations across the upper Midwest. Two weeks after the Q3 planning offsite, he sits with the facilitator's notes and the whiteboard photos, looking for what went wrong. Six hours, thirteen managers, one hired facilitator. The Q3 territory plan still does not exist. He works backward: the opening, the breakouts, the synthesis attempt that dissolved into hallway conversations. One root cause surfaces: the group never declared what the offsite needed to produce by 5 p.m.
examples.whatToDo: Before the next offsite, write one sentence naming the concrete deliverable: 'We leave with a written Q3 plan, assigned by territory, that each manager can act on Monday.' Post it at the front of the room.
examples.whyItMatters: A group without a declared outcome has no shared checkpoint. It cannot notice when discussion has drifted, cannot redirect itself, and cannot recognize when the work is actually finished.

examples.title: Luz Pictures the Finished Menu Insert Before Writing a Plan

planSpec.domain: a line cook asked to develop a new small-plates section for a seasonal menu change
planSpec.audience: a line cook at a mid-range restaurant who has cooked from other people's menus for three years but has never led development
planSpec.stakes: whether the chef's deadline is met or the cook hands in a vague draft of half-ideas that the chef has to rebuild from scratch
planSpec.requiredBeat: she imagines the printed menu with the section already complete — five dishes listed, portion notes included — and the image makes the first action obvious before any planning happens: write down five candidate dishes tonight before tomorrow's prep shift starts

examples.scenario: Luz has cooked from other people's menus for three years. The chef asks her to develop five small plates for the fall menu change, due Friday. She opens a notebook and waits. Nothing comes. Try the same move she finds: close your eyes and picture the finished menu insert, already laminated, sitting on a table in the dining room. Five dish names. A portion note beside each. A complete, real object. When the image settles, the gap between that picture and tonight is obvious, and it names the first thing to do.
examples.whatToDo: Picture the finished deliverable as a specific printed object before writing any plan. The image of what complete looks like surfaces the first gap: write down five candidate dishes tonight, before tomorrow's prep shift starts.
examples.whyItMatters: A blank page asks what to do next. A concrete image of the finished product asks only what is missing. The gap between the image and now is the work, and the nearest edge of that gap is always the next action.

questions.prompt: A line cook has been told to 'get the prep station ready for service.' She sits down to plan her next hour but cannot figure out where to start. What is the most useful thing she can do before picking the first task?
choices: Write one sentence describing what the prep station looks like when it is ready (mise en place complete, surfaces clear, fridge stocked for tonight's menu), then let the first task surface from that image.
Start with whatever feels most urgent and adjust as service time approaches.
Ask the chef to break the task into a specific list of steps before she touches anything.
questions.explanation: Without a declared close condition, 'ready' is undefined and any task feels equally valid or equally deferrable. Writing the outcome sentence makes the gap between now and done visible and the first task usually surfaces immediately. Starting from urgency and waiting for a chef's list both keep the vague framing in place.

questions.prompt: A software product team finishes sprint planning with twelve items on the board. Two weeks later, four items have been 'in progress' for the entire sprint without moving. The post-mortem surfaces a shared pattern in how those four were written. What pattern most likely explains the stall?
choices: The four items were assigned to developers who were also carrying the heaviest code-review load that sprint.
The four items described areas of ongoing work ('improve onboarding', 'fix search') rather than declaring a finished state, so no one could tell when they were done or what to do next.
The four items lacked clear owners listed in the ticket, causing coordination failures across the team.
questions.explanation: Items written as categories have no close condition, so any next step is equally defensible and there is no moment the item can logically stop. Ownership gaps and review load are real sprint problems but cannot explain why specifically these four stalled while eight others moved.

questions.prompt: An attorney adds 'handle the Henderson matter' to her task list. Three days later a colleague asks why the item is still untouched. What does the colleague's question expose about the entry?
choices: The attorney is avoiding the matter because the counterparty is difficult to work with.
The task list is too long for any single item to receive reliable attention during the week.
'Handle the Henderson matter' names an area of concern but declares no close condition, so there is no way to identify a first action or know when the commitment is satisfied.
questions.explanation: A task entry needs a close condition: a description of what the world looks like when the commitment is finished. 'Handle' describes activity, not a finished state, so no next action is obvious. Avoidance and list length are plausible guesses but cannot be inferred from the entry's wording alone.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit development director is choosing how to track her grant deadlines. Approach A lists each grant by funder name only. Approach B lists each grant with a declared outcome ('Foundation X application submitted with budget narrative and letters of support by March 15'). Which approach better supports a reliable tracking system, and why?
choices: Approach B, because the declared outcome provides a close condition that makes the next action identifiable at any point and signals clearly when each grant cycle is complete.
Approach A, because shorter list entries reduce cognitive load during a busy week and are faster to scan at a glance.
Both are equally valid: reliable tracking depends on how often the list is reviewed, not on how individual items are phrased.
questions.explanation: A funder name is a label, not a close condition. Approach B makes the next action identifiable at any moment and shows when each cycle is complete. Shorter entries scan faster but give no signal about what done looks like, and review frequency cannot substitute for a well-formed entry.

questions.prompt: A project architect writes 'coordinate with the structural engineer' on her project tracking sheet. Two weeks pass and nothing moves. What is the most effective revision she can make to this item?
choices: Break it into five sub-tasks covering every possible coordination topic so each piece is smaller and more approachable.
Move it to the top of the priority list so it receives attention before everything else each day.
Rewrite it as 'structural engineer confirms load-bearing wall specs signed off by November 3,' giving the item a close condition and making the first action obvious.
questions.explanation: A close condition makes the gap between now and done visible and usually surfaces a first action immediately (call or email the engineer). Breaking into sub-tasks and raising priority both preserve the vague framing and add noise without answering the question of what done looks like.

questions.prompt: A school principal launched six improvement initiatives in September. By late October, three are producing visible progress and three have stalled. She reviews how each was originally written to find what separates the two groups. What distinction most likely explains the pattern?
choices: The moving initiatives were led by teachers with more years of experience at the school.

The moving initiatives each had a declared end state ('all students receive written feedback within five days of each assessment') while the stalled ones used category labels ('improve assessment feedback') with no visible close condition.
The stalled initiatives were assigned to departments whose teams meet less frequently each week.
questions.explanation: A declared end state creates a close condition: progress is measurable and completion is visible. Category labels leave the loop open, so work continues without direction. Experience and meeting cadence are plausible factors but cannot explain why the labeling pattern so cleanly divides the two groups.

questions.prompt: A merchandise planner is about to start sourcing products for a holiday display. A colleague suggests spending ten minutes first to write one sentence declaring what the finished display looks like. The planner thinks this is overhead that slows the real work. Which view is correct?
choices: The colleague is right: without a declared outcome there is no close condition against which to evaluate candidate products or know when sourcing is complete.
The planner is right: experienced merchandisers carry the outcome in their heads, so the written sentence is redundant overhead.
Neither is fully right: the sentence is worth writing only if the display is unusually complex or the deadline is within three weeks.
questions.explanation: Without a close condition, sourcing has no stopping point and no clear filter for which products belong. Carrying the outcome in your head confuses familiarity with a trackable commitment. The complexity threshold is invented: close conditions help regardless of project size or deadline proximity.

questions.prompt: A clinic administrator has 'sort out the billing backlog' on her task list. At the end of a long day she sits down to work on it and cannot decide where to start. What is the most useful change she can make before picking any action?
choices: Reorganize the task list by due date so the billing item rises to the top of her attention.
Set a 25-minute timer and work on whatever billing task feels most approachable right now.
Write one sentence describing what the billing backlog looks like when it is resolved, then identify the first action that moves toward that state.
questions.explanation: The paralysis comes from a missing close condition: 'sort out' names an activity, not a finished state. Writing the outcome sentence makes the gap visible and a first action usually follows. List position addresses priority and a timer addresses energy, but neither provides a definition of done.

questions.prompt: A documentary producer reviews a project that has been 'in development' for four months with no pitch package completed. Both producers on the project say they have been working steadily. She reads the project description in the shared drive to diagnose the problem. What in the description most likely explains the stall?
choices: The description is stored in a shared folder that neither producer has opened consistently over the four months.
The description articulates themes and questions the film will explore but never declares what the finished pitch package contains, leaving no close condition for the work.
One producer's name is listed as primary contact, creating ambiguity about who is responsible for completing the package.
questions.explanation: A description of themes is a brief for exploration, not a declaration of what the pitch package contains. Without a close condition, steady work can continue in any direction without producing a deliverable. Shared-drive access and ownership ambiguity are logistical factors, not the structural gap.

reviewCards.front: You write 'deal with the Hendricks proposal' on your list. Before doing anything else, what is the move?
reviewCards.back: Declare what done looks like in one concrete sentence: 'Hendricks proposal revised, feedback incorporated, and PDF sent to the client by Friday.' Once a close condition exists outside your head, the next physical action surfaces on its own.

reviewCards.front: A charge nurse writes 'handle Room 14 discharge' on the shift whiteboard. The patient is medically cleared, but the room sits occupied two hours later. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The item was a category label, not an outcome. A close condition would read: 'patient has signed paperwork, transport is confirmed, and bed is flagged available.' That sentence makes the next phone call obvious and lets anyone on the floor see instantly whether the job is done.

reviewCards.front: Your team runs a full-day planning offsite. Six hours later, everyone leaves with no decisions made and no clear next steps. What is the most likely root cause?
reviewCards.back: No one declared what a successful offsite looked like before the room filled. Without a visible close condition, the group could not notice when it drifted, could not course-correct, and had no shared way to recognize when it was done. The missing piece was a single outcome sentence written before the first agenda item.

reviewCards.front: A line cook asked to develop five new small-plate dishes feels stuck, circling the same half-formed ideas for two days. What is the move that unsticks this kind of project?
reviewCards.back: Declare what done looks like before choosing any action: 'five dishes listed with portion notes, ready to hand to the chef before tomorrow's prep shift.' Visualize the finished menu page. The concrete image almost always makes the first action obvious, usually something small enough to start tonight.

reviewCards.front: You have carried 'revise the report' on your list for three weeks. Each time you look at it, you feel low-grade dread and skip it. What is the diagnosis and the fix?
reviewCards.back: The item is a category, not an outcome. Your system cannot track it because there is no close condition to check against. Write one sentence: what does the report look like when it is done, and by when? Once that sentence exists in the system, the next action usually becomes obvious, and the dread drops.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Outcome focusing is the habit of writing one concrete sentence that describes what done looks like before you decide what to do next. It turns vague commitments into items your system can actually track and close. Practiced consistently, it makes the gap between where you are and where you need to be visible and measurable. That visibility is what lets the next action surface on its own.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you are about to write a task that starts with 'handle,' 'deal with,' 'sort out,' or 'follow up on,' then stop and replace it with one sentence describing what the situation will look like when the commitment is fully closed, specific enough that a coworker could confirm it without asking you.

If an assignment or project has sat on your list for more than three days without any movement, then before opening any files write one sentence that names the finished artifact, its scope, and when it lands with whoever receives it.

If a conversation ends with you agreeing to 'figure something out' or 'get back to someone,' then before you add it to your system write exactly what you will hand them and by what date, so the commitment has a shape the other person could check.

If a health intention on your list still uses words like 'get better at,' 'improve,' or 'be more consistent,' then rewrite it as the specific condition that would let you say, without any doubt, that you are done with this particular commitment.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, open your task list or notes app and find one item that contains the word 'handle,' 'deal with,' or 'figure out.' Rewrite it as a single sentence describing what done looks like, concrete enough that someone else could check whether it is true.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, before your regular review, read each item on your active lists and ask: could I tell at a glance whether this is finished? Any item you cannot answer yes to gets rewritten as a close condition before you move on. This takes about ten minutes and keeps your list from filling with items that will never feel done.

memorableLines.text: The vagueness was not an accident. It was protection.
memorableLines.why: Reframes procrastination as self-protection rather than laziness, revealing the psychological reason people resist declaring what done actually means.

memorableLines.text: You cannot track a commitment that has no close condition, and most of yours do not have one.
memorableLines.why: Lands the problem personally and specifically, identifying the structural gap in the reader's own system that explains why commitments keep cycling.

memorableLines.text: The list does not need more items. It needs one sentence that says where this one ends.
memorableLines.why: Cuts through conventional list-making advice to name the actual missing piece—not more tasks but one precise close condition that makes the system trackable.
